[Labels in the figure: «Рис. 1» = Fig. 1]

Using a compass and a straightedge, construct the velocity vector of point $A$ and the acceleration vector of point $B$, briefly justifying the construction (describing standard constructions is not required). In the construction keep the proportions: the lengths of the segments representing the vectors (for example, the velocities) must be in the same ratio in the figure as the magnitudes of the corresponding physical quantities.

problems.title: Problem 2: Optical construction
problems.problem:
Problem 2: Optical construction

Fig. 2 shows three points $O$, $S_1$ and $S_2$ lying on one straight line. The point $O$ is the optical centre of an ideal converging lens, and the points $S_1$ and $S_2$ are a source and its image in this lens. An ideal lens is a thin lens in which any rays, including those at large angles to the optical axis, are refracted as paraxial ones.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/moscow-2026-4-2-fig1.png
[Labels in the figure: «Рис. 2» = Fig. 2]

Using a compass and a straightedge, determine the position of the focus of the lens nearest to $S_1$ in the case when the line $OS_1S_2$ is its principal optical axis.

Construct the locus of points where one of the foci of this lens may be located if the position of its principal optical axis in the plane of the figure is arbitrary.

Briefly justify the constructions performed (standard constructions need no justification).

problems.title: Problem 3: Common emitter
problems.problem:
Problem 3: Common emitter

A bipolar $npn$ transistor is a semiconductor device with three terminals: the emitter, the collector and the base. These terminals are labelled with the corresponding letters in the diagram in Fig. 3, which shows a simplified amplifier stage on a transistor. This circuit is designed to increase the amplitude of a signal, that is, of the alternating component of the input voltage. If the input is supplied with a voltage of the form

$$U_{\mathrm{in}}(t)=U_{\mathrm{bias}}+U_1\sin(\omega t),$$

where $U_{\mathrm{bias}}$ (the base bias voltage) and $\omega$ (the angular frequency) are constants and $U_1$ is the signal amplitude, then the voltage across the high-resistance load $R_{\mathrm{L}}$ connected to the output (between the emitter and the collector) also contains a constant and an alternating component. The output signal has an almost sinusoidal shape (the distortion usually does not exceed a few percent), and its amplitude $U_2$ is several times larger than the amplitude of the input signal $U_1$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/moscow-2026-4-3-fig1.png
[Labels in the figure: «Рис. 3» = Fig. 3; «U_вх» = $U_{\mathrm{in}}$; «U_вых» = $U_{\mathrm{out}}$; «R_н» = $R_{\mathrm{L}}$; «I_б», «I_к», «I_э» = $I_{\mathrm{B}}$, $I_{\mathrm{C}}$, $I_{\mathrm{E}}$; «б», «к», «э» = B (base), C (collector), E (emitter)]

The main characteristic of an amplifier stage is the voltage gain, the modulus of the ratio of the amplitudes of the output and input signals:

$$K_U=\left|\frac{U_2}{U_1}\right|.$$

Let the base bias voltage and the input signal amplitude be $U_{\mathrm{bias}}=0.7\ \mathrm{V}$ and $U_1=0.2\ \mathrm{mV}$ respectively.

The input characteristic of the transistor, that is, the dependence of the base current $I_{\mathrm{B}}$ on the base–emitter voltage $U_{\mathrm{BE}}$, is given by the relation

$$I_{\mathrm{B}}=I_{\mathrm{B0}}\cdot10^{\left(\frac{U_{\mathrm{BE}}}{U_T}-12\right)}.$$

Here $U_T=0.06\ \mathrm{V}$, $I_{\mathrm{B0}}=5\ \mathrm{\mu A}$. For clarity, Fig. 4 shows the graph of this dependence for voltages close to the base bias voltage.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/moscow-2026-4-3-fig2.png
[Labels in the figure: «Рис. 4» = Fig. 4; «I_б, мкА» = $I_{\mathrm{B}}$, $\mathrm{\mu A}$; «U_бэ, В» = $U_{\mathrm{BE}}$, V]

The dependence of the collector current $I_{\mathrm{C}}$ on the collector–emitter voltage $U_{\mathrm{CE}}$ in the range of currents and voltages considered depends parametrically on the base current $I_{\mathrm{B}}$ and is described by the formula

$$I_{\mathrm{C}}=200\cdot I_{\mathrm{B}}\left(1+\frac{U_{\mathrm{CE}}}{U_A}\right),$$

where $U_A=100\ \mathrm{V}$. The resistance of the rheostat $R$ in the circuit in Fig. 3 can vary from $1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ to $10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$, and the voltage of the ideal source is $U_0=9\ \mathrm{V}$. The current through the load $R_{\mathrm{L}}$ is negligible compared with the collector current.

Determine, for the extreme values of the rheostat resistance, the collector current $I_{\mathrm{C0}}$ in the absence of an input alternating signal ($U_1=0$).

The current gain $K_I=I_{\mathrm{C}}/I_{\mathrm{B}}$ depends only weakly on the base current for the given parameters. Determine $K_I$ with an accuracy of no worse than $1.0\%$ for $R=5\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$.

What values can the voltage gain $K_U$ take? State the boundaries of the possible range with an accuracy of no worse than $2.0\%$. Within this model such accuracy is attainable even taking into account the small distortions of the output signal.

Note: It is possible (but not obligatory) that in solving this you will need the formula for the derivative of the function $f(x)=10^x$ at the point $x=x_0$:

$$(10^x)'\Big|_{x=x_0}=\ln 10\cdot10^{x_0}\approx2.302585\cdot10^{x_0}.$$

problems.title: Problem 4: The bead and the load
problems.problem:
Problem 4: The bead and the load

A small massive bead of mass $m$ is threaded on a smooth wire ring of radius $R$ fixed in a vertical plane. One end of a thin inextensible massless thread is attached to the bead (see Fig. 5). Its other end is passed through a small ideal pulley and attached to a load of mass $km$, where $k$ is a constant coefficient. The pulley is fixed at a point lying on the horizontal diameter of the ring. The position of the bead on the ring is characterised by the angle $\varphi$ between the directions from the centre of the ring to the pulley and to the bead.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/moscow-2026-4-4-fig1.png
[Labels in the figure: «Рис. 5» = Fig. 5]

Let $k=1/\sqrt{3}$. Determine the angle (or angles) corresponding to the equilibrium position of the bead.

At the initial moment the bead, which is in a position of stable equilibrium, is given a speed $v$ by a blow, directed along the ring away from the pulley. At what minimal value of the speed $v=v_{\min}$ will the bead be able to reach the pulley, moving all the time in one direction (clockwise)?

For what values of the parameter $k$ are there no points on the ring at which the bead could be in a state of stable equilibrium?

Now let there be friction between the bead and the wire, and let the coefficient of friction depend on the angle as $\mu=\tan(\varphi/2)$. For the case of equal masses ($k=1$), does there exist a position of stable equilibrium with $\varphi\in\left(0;\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$? Find this position (or positions) or prove that none exists.

The dimensions of the ring mounting, the pulley, the bead and the load may be neglected. The thread is long enough that the load does not collide with the pulley while the bead moves. In Fig. 5 the proportions are changed for clarity. The free-fall acceleration is $g$.

problems.title: Problem 5: In the flow
problems.problem:
Problem 5: In the flow

This problem considers the effect of condensation of water vapour in regions of reduced pressure that arise when a flow of humid air passes around obstacles. Because of this effect, a so-called «vapour cone» may appear near the trailing edge of the wings and along the fuselage of an aircraft.

Further, a steady adiabatic flow of an inviscid ideal gas is considered. This means that the flow parameters at each point do not change with time, there is no heat exchange, and internal friction can be neglected.

The Mach number $\mathrm{M}=\frac{v}{c}$ is the ratio of the flow speed $v$ at some point to the speed of sound $c$ at the same point. The speed of sound is given by the formula

$$c=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{\mu}}.$$

Consider air to be an ideal gas with adiabatic index $\gamma=\frac{c_P}{c_V}=\frac{7}{5}$ and molar mass $\mu=29\ \mathrm{g/mol}$. The adiabatic process is described by the equation $P\rho^{-\gamma}=\mathrm{const}$, where $P$ is the pressure and $\rho$ is the density.

Also consider known the relation expressing the law of conservation of energy for a steady flow (Bernoulli's equation for a compressible gas):

$$\frac{v^2}{2}+\frac{c_PT}{\mu}=\mathrm{const}.$$

An aircraft flies in air at temperature $T_0=295\ \mathrm{K}$ and pressure $P_0=101.325\ \mathrm{kPa}$. In the frame of reference of the aircraft the speed of the oncoming flow far from it corresponds to the Mach number $\mathrm{M}_0=0.35$. In flowing around the wings and some parts of the fuselage the air speed increases, reaching a maximum value corresponding to $\mathrm{M}_{\max}=0.5$.

At what maximum value of the relative humidity $\varphi_{\max}$ of the surrounding air is the formation of a vapour cone impossible? The dependence of the saturated water vapour pressure on temperature is shown in Fig. 6 (see sheet 3).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/moscow-2026-4-5-fig1.png
[Labels in the figure: «Рис. 6: Зависимость давления насыщенного пара воды от температуры, к задаче 5» = Fig. 6: Dependence of the saturated water vapour pressure on temperature, for Problem 5; «P, кПа» = $P$, kPa; «T, К» = $T$, K]

problems.title: Problem 1: Turning the system around
problems.problem:
Problem 1: Turning the system around

Two piers are located on opposite banks of a river of width $100\ \mathrm{m}$, directly opposite each other, at points $A$ and $B$. The speed of the river current is $1\ \mathrm{m/s}$. On the same bank as pier $B$, downstream, there is pier $C$. A rowing boat leaves pier $A$, keeping its heading at an angle $\alpha$ ($\sin\alpha=3/5$) to the direction of the velocity of the river current. The speed of the boat relative to the water remains constant in magnitude and direction all the time. At the same time as the boat, a cyclist sets off from pier $B$ towards pier $C$ and moves with constant speed. Having reached pier $C$, he quickly turns round by $180^\circ$ and rides back towards pier $B$ with the same speed.

Fig. 1 shows (to an unknown scale) the trajectory $KLMN$ of the boat in the frame of reference of the cyclist from the moment of departure (point $K$) to the moment of landing on the opposite bank (point $N$). The axes of the coordinate system used are rigidly attached to the frame of the bicycle (not shown in the figure). The cyclist's turn by $180^\circ$ is considered instantaneous.

Determine the speed of the cyclist, the speed of the boat relative to the water and the distance between the piers $B$ and $C$.

problems.title: Problem 2: Friction and a neural network
problems.problem:
Problem 2: Friction and a neural network

A massive triangular prism of mass $m=1\ \mathrm{kg}$, whose cross-section is a right triangle with acute angle $\alpha$, is held on a rough inclined plane with angle of inclination $\alpha$ to the horizontal ($\tan\alpha=1/2$). The prism lies on the plane on a lateral face such that its other lateral face (facing up) is horizontal. A sheet of paper lies on this face, and a block of mass $m$ lies on the sheet of paper. The block is connected by a thread (massless and inextensible) to a very light ring put on a smooth vertical fixed rod (see Fig. 2). The thread is not taut, but does not sag either, so that horizontal motion of the block (if the system is released) is excluded for some time.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/moscow-2026-6-2-fig1.png
[Labels in the figure: «Рис. 2» = Fig. 2]

The coefficients of friction of the prism against the paper and of the block against the paper are equal and equal to $\mu_1$. The coefficient of friction of the prism against the inclined plane is $\mu_2$. It is assumed that $0\leqslant\mu_1\leqslant1$ and $0\leqslant\mu_2\leqslant1$. The system is released.

For which $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ will the wedge begin to move? Draw in the $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ plane the region corresponding to the values found.

Below is the solution of the first part of the problem proposed by a well-known neural network. Is it correct? If yes, it can be used; if not, point out the mistakes made.

The block is held by the thread and has no horizontal acceleration. Consequently, the friction force between the block and the paper balances the horizontal reaction from the prism. The maximum friction force between the block and the paper is

$$F_{1,\max}=\mu_1mg.$$

The same in magnitude force acts on the prism from the paper (in the opposite direction) and is directed horizontally. The following act on the prism: its weight $mg$, the weight of the block $mg$, the normal reaction of the plane $N_2$ and the friction force on the plane $F_2$.

The total normal reaction of the inclined plane

$$N_2=2mg\cos\alpha.$$

The maximum friction force of the prism on the plane

$$F_{2,\max}=2\mu_2mg\cos\alpha.$$

The component of the forces tending to move the prism down the inclined plane: $2mg\sin\alpha$. The horizontal friction force from the paper gives a projection onto the inclined plane: $F_{1,\parallel}=F_1\cos\alpha$. In the limiting case $F_1=\mu_1mg$, therefore

$$F_{1,\parallel}=\mu_1mg\cos\alpha.$$

Condition for the start of sliding of the prism:

$$2mg\sin\alpha-\mu_1mg\cos\alpha>2\mu_2mg\cos\alpha.$$

Dividing by $mg\cos\alpha$, we get

$$2\tan\alpha-\mu_1>2\mu_2.$$

For $\tan\alpha=\frac{1}{2}$ finally

$$1-\mu_1>2\mu_2,\qquad\mu_2<\frac{1-\mu_1}{2}.$$

Thus the prism will begin to slip out when

$$\mu_2<\frac{1-\mu_1}{2},\qquad0\leq\mu_1\leq1,\ 0\leq\mu_2\leq1.$$

In the $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ plane this is the region below the line

$$\mu_2=\frac{1-\mu_1}{2}.$$

problems.title: Problem 3: The Magnus effect
problems.problem:
Problem 3: The Magnus effect

In ball games, spin shots are widely used, in which the ball is given not only a translational velocity but also rotation. As a result the ball moves along a complicated trajectory and under certain conditions deviates sideways from the vertical plane containing the initial velocity vector.

Such a trajectory of the ball is explained by the Magnus effect. The interaction of the rotating ball with the air is quantitatively characterised by two forces: the drag force $F_{\mathrm{D}}$ (directed opposite to the velocity of the centre of the ball) and the Magnus force $F_{\mathrm{M}}$, directed perpendicular to the velocity (see Fig. 3) and also perpendicular to the axis of rotation. In this problem the axis of rotation is assumed to be perpendicular to the direction of the velocity of the centre of the ball.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/moscow-2026-6-3-fig1.png
[Labels in the figure: «Рис. 3» = Fig. 3]

To a first approximation these forces can be taken to be given by the formulas

$$F_{\mathrm{D}}=C_{\mathrm{D}}v^2,\qquad F_{\mathrm{M}}=C_{\mathrm{M}}\omega v,$$

where $C_{\mathrm{D}}$ and $C_{\mathrm{M}}$ are constant coefficients, $v$ is the speed of the centre of the ball, and $\omega$ is the angular velocity of its rotation (it is assumed that it does not change during the flight).

The analysis of the motion of a rotating body in a gravitational field in the presence of aerodynamic forces is rather complicated. Therefore below we neglect gravity and restrict ourselves to considering the planar motion of the ball under the action of only two forces: the drag $F_{\mathrm{D}}$ and the Magnus force $F_{\mathrm{M}}$.

Let $C_{\mathrm{D}}=0$, that is, there is no drag force. The quantities $C_{\mathrm{M}}$, $\omega$ and $m$ are known. The ball leaves the point $A$ with speed $v_0$ at an angle $\alpha=30^\circ$ to a horizontal straight line. Find the distance $AB$, where $B$ is the point where the trajectory intersects this line again.

In this part $C_{\mathrm{D}}\neq0$. A ball of mass $m=3\ \mathrm{g}$ leaves with speed $v_0=15\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at an angle $\alpha=30^\circ$ to the vertical. The angular velocity of rotation is $\omega=100\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. The trajectory of the ball over the time interval $t_0=0.5\ \mathrm{s}$ is shown in Fig. 4. This graph was obtained by numerical simulation; a copy of the graph is given on sheet 4, see Fig. 7.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/moscow-2026-6-3-fig2.png
[Labels in the figure: «Рис. 4» = Fig. 4; «y, м» = $y$, m; «x, м» = $x$, m]

The dependence of the speed of the ball on time $v(t)$ over the same interval is given in Fig. 5 (see the next sheet). Using the graphs, determine the coefficients $C_{\mathrm{D}}$ and $C_{\mathrm{M}}$ with the greatest possible accuracy.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/moscow-2026-6-3-fig3.png
[Labels in the figure: «Рис. 5» = Fig. 5; «v, м/с» = $v$, m/s; «t, с» = $t$, s]

Note: The mass of 3 g and the stated kinematic parameters are typical of a table tennis ball in spin shots of medium strength.

problems.title: Problem 4: Nonlinear elements
problems.problem:
Problem 4: Nonlinear elements

Consider nonlinear elements $Z_1$ and $Z_2$, whose resistance depends on the voltage across their terminals.

As the voltage across element $Z_1$ is increased from zero, its resistance is $100\ \Omega$ up to $1.999\ \mathrm{V}$. In the narrow interval from $1.999\ \mathrm{V}$ to $2.001\ \mathrm{V}$ it increases linearly to $200\ \Omega$, after which it remains constant. The resistance of element $Z_2$ changes in the opposite way: up to $1.999\ \mathrm{V}$ it is $200\ \Omega$, in the interval from $1.999\ \mathrm{V}$ to $2.001\ \mathrm{V}$ it decreases linearly to $100\ \Omega$ and does not change further.

In analysing the circuit the finite width of the transition region must be taken into account. However, in plotting the final graphs this width ($0.002\ \mathrm{V}$) may be neglected.

Draw the current–voltage characteristics of the elements $Z_1$ and $Z_2$. Recall that the current–voltage characteristic (I–V curve) is the dependence of the current flowing through an element on the voltage across it (the current is plotted on the ordinate axis, the voltage on the abscissa axis). Consider only positive values of these quantities; mark the coordinates of the break points on the graphs.

The elements $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ are connected in series and connected to an adjustable voltage source. Starting from some moment, the voltage across the terminals of this connection increases uniformly from zero and reaches $6\ \mathrm{V}$ after one minute. Then it decreases in the same uniform way and becomes zero again by the end of the second minute of the experiment.

Draw the graph of the current in the circuit as a function of time $I(t)$. On the graph the coordinates of the break points, as well as of the local maxima and minima of the current, must be marked.
